red.summary: An event happening before another does not prove the first produced the second. Learn to build a causal argument from observations, plausible mechanisms and alternative explanations.
checklist: I can recognize the post hoc fallacy
I can distinguish correlation from causation
I can identify a fact that could test competing explanations

sections.title: After Does Not Mean Because
sections.body_md: A city installs cameras, then theft declines. The order of events is real, but it does not establish that cameras caused the change. Weather, new patrols or reporting practices could also matter. The post hoc fallacy treats 'after this' as proof of 'because of this.' Legal advocacy should distinguish a timeline from a demonstrated effect. Ask what evidence supports the claimed connection and what alternative changes occurred at the same time.

Legal advocacy should distinguish a timeline from a demonstrated effect. Ask what evidence supports the claimed connection and what alternative changes occurred at the same time.

sections.title: A Cause Needs a Reasoned Link
sections.body_md: A mechanic finds that a vehicle's brakes failed before a collision. That observation may support a causal theory, but inspection records and the sequence of events still matter. A clear argument identifies conduct, outcome and evidence connecting them. The conclusion should be no stronger than that connection allows. In law, an additional question may arise: whether the governing liability rule assigns responsibility for the harm. Physical explanation and legal attribution are related but distinct.

sections.title: Ask What Would Have Happened Otherwise
sections.body_md: A useful counterfactual question asks what likely would have happened without the suspected action. If a traffic signal had worked, might the collision still have occurred? This cannot always be known with certainty, but it focuses investigation on facts that discriminate between hypotheses. The beginner need not use elaborate statistics. The important habit is to avoid accepting the first explanation merely because it is emotionally compelling or easy to describe.

yellow.focus: Use necessary and sufficient conditions without causal confusion
yellow.summary: Causal explanations often involve several contributors and different logical relationships. Distinguish what is required for an outcome from what could produce it alone.
checklist: I can explain necessity and sufficiency in a causal argument
I can identify multiple sufficient causes
I can avoid converting correlation into a legal rule

sections.title: One Condition May Not Be Enough
sections.body_md: A fire requires fuel, oxygen and ignition in a simplified physical model. Having fuel alone is not sufficient for a fire, even though fuel is a necessary part of that model. Legal reasoning also distinguishes conditions from complete explanations. A shop's failure to inspect may increase risk without being the sole reason an injury occurred. Define the relevant outcome and scope of the claim before deciding whether a fact was necessary, sufficient or only contributory.

Define the relevant outcome and scope of the claim before deciding whether a fact was necessary, sufficient or only contributory.

sections.title: Two Causes May Each Suffice
sections.body_md: Imagine two independent fires merging and destroying a house. If either fire alone would have destroyed it, an ordinary but-for inquiry applied to each may misleadingly suggest neither was necessary. This is causal overdetermination. Legal systems handle such problems differently under specified liability doctrines. The student must first recognize the logical difficulty, then find the governing legal response. It is unsafe to assert one universal multiple-cause rule without checking jurisdiction.

It is unsafe to assert one universal multiple-cause rule without checking jurisdiction.

sections.title: Evidence Is Not the Same as a Formal Implication
sections.body_md: A study might associate a chemical exposure with illness while other variables influence both. The statement 'if exposed, then ill' is often too strong and may erase probabilities. A lawyer should preserve the actual scientific claim and avoid turning risk into a deterministic rule. The causal argument must explain what evidence exists, what alternatives were considered and which legal proof requirement applies. Good logic prevents both false accusations and the dismissal of real injury.

orange.focus: Evaluate counterfactual reasoning and selection effects
orange.summary: Advanced causal arguments can fail because the comparison group is biased or because investigators condition on the wrong variable. Learn to state assumptions instead of disguising them as conclusions.
checklist: I can identify a confounder in an observational claim
I can explain a selection effect on causal estimates
I can distinguish association from a legal causal proposition

sections.title: The Unseen Comparison
sections.body_md: A new legal advice program is associated with higher success rates, but the participants were more motivated or better resourced than those who did not participate. Those differences can affect both participation and outcomes. An observational comparison therefore needs a defensible counterfactual strategy. Legal arguments using such evidence should state what would have to be true for a causal interpretation. Calling an analysis rigorous does not remove the need to examine its selection mechanism.

sections.title: Selection Can Create a False Link
sections.body_md: Suppose a study includes only people admitted to a specialist clinic. Both severe symptoms and access to insurance affect admission. Looking only at admitted patients may produce misleading associations between those factors, even when they were unrelated in the broader population. This kind of selection or collider bias can make a causal story appear stronger than the evidence warrants. The analyst should draw the data-selection process before drawing conclusions about a defendant's responsibility.

sections.title: Inference and Legal Burden Are Different
sections.body_md: An expert may report a plausible causal relationship with uncertainty, while a tribunal must decide whether the proof satisfies a particular legal standard. Those are not identical judgments. The lawyer should identify which empirical question the analysis answers, which assumptions it relies on, and how the applicable rule allocates uncertainty. The best argument explains strengths and weaknesses plainly instead of transforming a model output into an automatic verdict.

black.focus: Critique formal causal models under legal and moral uncertainty
black.summary: At doctoral depth, assess what a causal model can establish, what its assumptions conceal and which consequences belong to normative legal choice. Defend a fair approach to multi-actor harms.
checklist: I can evaluate the assumptions in structural causal models
I can distinguish causal contribution from legal responsibility
I can defend procedures to correct high-stakes causal errors

sections.title: Models Depend on Assumptions
sections.body_md: A structural causal model represents relationships among variables, often with equations or a diagram. The graphical clarity can reveal assumptions but does not prove that those assumptions describe reality. Unobserved confounding, measurement error and misspecified mechanisms can change estimated effects. A doctoral lawyer must ask who selected variables, what alternative models fit the evidence and which assumptions can be tested. A precise calculation based on false premises is not reliable proof of responsibility.

Unobserved confounding, measurement error and misspecified mechanisms can change estimated effects. A doctoral lawyer must ask who selected variables, what alternative models fit the evidence and which assumptions can be tested. A precise calculation based on false premises is not reliable proof of responsibility.

sections.title: Responsibility Is Not Only Physics
sections.body_md: Even when a model establishes that an actor's conduct contributed to harm, the governing legal system determines which harms are attributable and which remedies follow. Multiple sufficient causes, long chains and collective institutions make the distinction more important. A moral argument that someone should bear a loss is not the same as the legal proposition that the person does. Scholarly rigor requires disclosing where an empirical conclusion ends and a normative assignment of responsibility begins.

sections.title: Build Reviewability Into Inference
sections.body_md: If algorithmic risk scores influence detention, health benefits or regulatory sanctions, affected persons need intelligible reasons and lawful opportunities to challenge the evidence. A doctoral proposal should specify data provenance, independent validation, error measurement and review procedures. It must consider whom false positives and false negatives harm and how those risks are distributed. Legal causal reasoning reaches maturity when sophisticated models remain answerable to human beings rather than becoming unchallengeable sources of coercion.
